title: The Sri Yantra: a Home Drawn in Lines
hookLine: can a drawing be a home for the divine?
carry: the sri yantra is the goddess's home and form
tomorrow: a wall around a home, with a gate in every side. why?
last: WORSHIP WAS NEVER ONLY ON THE SHELF.

lines: CAN A DRAWING BE A HOME?
cards: Unpacking a home shrine, things come out of the newspaper one at a time: a lamp, a bell, a small framed picture of a god. Then a flat brass plate with no face on it at all.
Just lines: triangles crossing triangles, rings of petals, a square border with a gate on each side, and a tiny point in the middle. And it gets the same flowers as everything else on the shelf.
So, one question for today: can a drawing be a home for the divine?

teach.h: THE SRI YANTRA: HER HOME AND FORM.
teach.b: This is the Sri Yantra, also called the Sri Chakra. A yantra is a diagram used in worship and meditation, and this one is at the heart of Sri Vidya, a way of worship centered on the Goddess as Lalita Tripurasundari.
Her thousand names, the Lalita Sahasranama, include one that answers today's question: she is the one whose home is the Sri Chakra, king of chakras.
So for those who worship with it, the yantra isn't decoration, and it isn't a reminder of someone absent. It's treated as her dwelling and her form, drawn in geometry instead of painted with a face.
A neighbor tradition asks a close cousin of this question.

teach.h: EXODUS: A SANCTUARY TO DWELL IN.
teach.b: In the book of Exodus, read by Jews and Christians, God tells Moses: "And let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them." Then God shows Moses a pattern, and the tabernacle is built to it, measure by measure.

teach.h: SHARED: A MADE PLACE FOR THE HOLY.
teach.b: Here's what the two share: a made thing, built with care to a given design, as a place where the holy is among people. And the honest difference.
In Exodus, nothing in the sanctuary is made to be God's form; the commandments say, "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image."
In Sri Vidya, the lines themselves are honored as the Goddess's form. Two old answers to one question, each in its own words.

how: In Sri Vidya homes and temples the Sri Yantra, drawn, engraved on metal or carved, receives flowers, kumkum and lamps as the Goddess's dwelling. Jews and Christians read of the tabernacle in Exodus as the sanctuary built so God would dwell among the people.

games.q: a classmate says it's silly to treat any made object as holy. which answer stays true to both texts you heard today?
o: Exodus has a sanctuary made so God may dwell among people; Sri Vidya honors the yantra as her home.
both texts agree that nothing made by human hands can ever be holy.
both texts teach that the made object is God's own face and body.
games.why: both have a made place for the holy, built with care. they differ on form: Exodus forbids an image; Sri Vidya honors the lines as the Goddess's form.

practice: If there's paper and a pen nearby, draw a small square, a triangle inside it, and a dot at the center, slowly, with no need to be neat. Then rest your eyes on the dot for the rest of the sit.
If you pray, you can let the drawing be a small place for the one you pray to; if not, let it be a place for your attention to come home.
